curriculum.lesson_evidence: A drawing line can change when you change the pressure on your pencil, the speed of your hand or the way you move. Pressing lightly makes a thin, pale line and pressing harder makes a thick, dark one. Wavy lines suggest water or hair, zigzags suggest lightning or spikes, and hatching, a set of short parallel lines, can fill an area to look darker. Hold the pencil loosely, relax your shoulder and draw from your arm, not just your fingers.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
You want to draw a calm lake with a thundercloud above it. Choose a line type for the water and a different one for the cloud, and say how you would change the pressure for each.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: 'Long wavy lines pressed lightly for the calm water, and thick zigzag lines pressed hard for the dark cloud.' The soft pressure suggests quiet, and the hard pressure makes the cloud feel heavy and stormy.

WATCH FOR
Believing that you must keep a pencil line neat and straight to be a good drawer. Experimenting with different pressures, speeds and line types is how artists find effects, and rubbing out too early stops you learning.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Fill a page with a line chart: draw six boxes and fill each with a different line (thick, thin, wavy, zigzag, hatching, spiral). Then draw a rainy street using at least three of your lines, and label where you used each and what it shows.

Write a short reflection naming one artistic choice you changed and why. Movement or instrument work is optional, adult-supervised and can be described instead.

teaching.why: This helps the learner make intentional visual, music, drama or dance choices and name their effect, rather than saying an artwork is simply “nice”. Keep every claim linked to an element or technique.

visuals.teaches: Pick a line for the job.
